newsitem.title: PERU: Early talks yield no results in Peru rebel siege.
newsitem.headline: Early talks yield no results in Peru rebel siege.

text.p: First negotiations brought no breakthrough on Thursday in the hostage crisis in Peru where leftist rebels have threatened to kill hundreds of captives in the Japanese ambassador's residence.

"The gentlemen of the MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement) inform that a diligent mediation is being carried out ... by representatives of the Red Cross," said Canada's ambassador, Anthony Vincent, one of five diplomats released on Wednesday by the rebels to act as a negotiating channel.

Vincent spoke to reporters after spending about 30 minutes apparently talking to the rebels at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, which MRTA guerrillas stormed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday night.
The Canadian, who earlier held a two-hour meeting with Peru's mediator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo Cabrejos, did not give any more details of the negotiating process.

The rebels -- holding up to 484 people including many high-ranking diplomats, businessmen and government officials -- have demanded the release of 400 to 500 imprisoned comrades and the presence of President Alberto Fujimori for talks. They said if the demands were not met they would kill the hostages.

Red Cross representative Michel Minning, who also went into the compound for about 20 minutes, told reporters afterwards those inside were "fine, all calm." He said they immediately needed food and toiletries. "We will address the question of the negotiations later," he added.
Witnesses said three men with shirt sleeves rolled up were chatting and looking out from behind a barred first-floor window, but it was unclear if they were rebels or hostages.

Governments around the world have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything it can to protect the hostages. The embassy residence is legally Japanese territory, meaning in theory Fujimori would need Tokyo's approval for an assault.
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda was due to arrive from Tokyo later on Thursday to help in the negotiations.

The German government, whose ambassador was released on Wednesday, urged Fujimori not to reject any chance to speak to the guerrillas. "I appeal to you not to rule out any possibility for discussion which would lead to a peaceful conclusion," Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said in a telegram to Fujimori.

The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to assist the U.S. ambassador to Peru in the crisis, the State Department said. The ambassador and his deputy were at the reception but left before the guerrillas struck. The State Department refused to comment on reports that six U.S. officials were among the hostages.
Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence on Wednesday, held his third emergency cabinet meeting since the crisis began.

The president, in his second term, had won an apparent victory over leftist rebels who fought a 16-year war against the government, jailing the leadership of the Cuban-inspired MRTA and the better-known Maoist Shining Path. But the MRTA showed it was far from dead with the daring attack.

The rebels assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters in a cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the residence beforehand among flowers and inside Christmas cake.

The rebels released Fujimori's mother and sister along with other women but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, may have narrowly escaped himself. He apparently was to attend the party but was delayed on a trip to the provinces.

Guerrilla spokesmen said they attacked the Japanese ambassador's home to protest Tokyo's support for Fujimori and his economic policies. Japan was chosen "due to the constant meddling of the Japanese government in Peru," the rebels said.

Japan, Austria, Spain, South Korea, Panama, Malaysia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Guatemala and Honduras confirmed their ambassadors were among the hostages, along with British and U.S. embassy officials.

Red Cross officials took supplies of food, water and an X-ray machine into the residence. Peru's largest human rights group said it had received a communication from the hostages warning the health of some was in danger, but Peruvian cameraman Juan Victor Sumarriba, who was allowed into the residence, said the hostages were walking around and talking among themselves freely.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president, and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.
MRTA and Shining Path attempts to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
